title: 22. Interview: OAuth 2.0
summary: Interview Q&A for OAuth 2.0 — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 OAuth 2.0 interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What problem does OAuth 2.0 solve that password-sharing did not?
**Answer:** Before OAuth, third-party apps that wanted to access a user's data on another service had to ask the user for their password on that service. This was catastrophic: the app could do anything the user could do (including changing the password), the app saw everything rather than the specific data it needed, and the user had no way to revoke access short of changing their password. OAuth 2.0 replaces password sharing with delegation: the user authenticates only with their identity provider, the provider issues a scoped, short-lived access token to the third-party app, and the app uses the token to access only the resources the user authorized. The user can revoke the token at any time without changing their password, the app never sees the password, and the granted scope limits what the app can do. "Log in with Google" and "Sign in with Apple" are the dominant consumer implementations; billions of daily authentications rely on this pattern.
**Visual:**
```
BAD (password sharing):
  app <-- password --> service
  app can do EVERYTHING user can

GOOD (OAuth 2.0):
  user -> AS (authenticates)
  AS  -> app (scoped access token)
  app -> RS (only authorized scope)
  user can revoke token anytime
```

### Q2. What are the four OAuth roles, and how do they map to a real "Log in with Google" flow?
**Answer:** The four roles are the resource owner (the user), the client (the third-party app requesting access), the authorization server (Google's accounts.google.com, which authenticates the user and issues tokens), and the resource server (Google's APIs — Gmail, Calendar, Drive). In a typical flow: the user clicks "Log in with Google" in the client; the client redirects the user to accounts.google.com; the user authenticates and approves the requested scopes; Google redirects back to the client with an authorization code; the client exchanges the code at Google's token endpoint for an access token; the client uses the access token to call Google's APIs to read the user's profile or email. Note that when OAuth is used for login (not just API access), OpenID Connect layers identity on top — the access token alone does not tell the client who the user is.
**Visual:**
```
user (resource owner)
   |
   v
client app  --redirect-->  Google AS (accounts.google.com)
   ^                          |
   | code                     | user logs in + consents
   |                          v
   +---exchange code for token---> access_token
   |
   v
Google RS (gmail.googleapis.com)  <-- Bearer access_token
```

### Q3. What is PKCE, and why is it now required for SPAs and mobile apps?
**Answer:** PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) replaces the static `client_secret` with a per-request challenge/verifier pair. The client generates a random `code_verifier` (43–128 characters), computes `code_challenge = base64url(sha256(verifier))`, and sends the challenge in the `/authorize` request. The authorization server stores the challenge alongside the issued code. When the client redeems the code at `/token`, it sends the verifier; the server hashes it and compares to the stored challenge, accepting only if they match. PKCE matters for SPAs and mobile apps because these clients cannot keep a static secret — anything compiled into JavaScript or an app binary is extractable. Without PKCE, an attacker who intercepts the authorization code (via a malicious redirect_uri, browser history, or mobile custom-scheme interception) can redeem it without the secret. With PKCE, the attacker also needs the verifier, which the client never put on the wire to `/authorize`. Google, Microsoft, GitHub, and Auth0 require PKCE for SPA and mobile clients as of 2023.
**Visual:**
```
client generates verifier V (random)
challenge C = SHA-256(V)

/authorize?code_challenge=C  --> server stores (code, C)
/token?code=X&verifier=V     --> server checks SHA-256(V) == C
                                  (attacker lacks V, cannot redeem code)
```

### Q4. What is the difference between the authorization code, implicit, password, and client credentials flows, and which should you use?
**Answer:** Authorization code with PKCE is the only flow recommended for new applications in 2024 — the user authenticates at the authorization server, the server returns a code via the front channel, the client exchanges the code (plus PKCE verifier) for tokens at the back channel. The implicit flow returned the access token directly in the redirect URL fragment; deprecated because tokens in URLs leak via browser history and referrer headers, and because implicit cannot issue refresh tokens safely. The resource owner password credentials (ROPC) flow let the client collect the user's password and exchange it directly for a token; deprecated in OAuth 2.1 because it defeats delegation. The client credentials flow is for service-to-service authentication with no user — a backend service authenticates with its own `client_id` and `client_secret` (or mTLS) and receives an access token scoped to its own identity. Use authorization code with PKCE for any user-facing client; use client credentials for service-to-service; do not use implicit or ROPC for new code.
**Visual:**
```
auth code + PKCE  : web/SPA/mobile (user-facing) -- USE THIS
implicit          : deprecated (token in URL, leaks)
password (ROPC)   : deprecated (client sees password)
client credentials: service-to-service (no user)
device grant      : CLI/TV without keyboard
```

### Q5. What are scopes, and how should a client request them?
**Answer:** Scopes are string identifiers that the client requests and the user approves, defining what the issued access token can do at the resource server. Examples include `calendar.read`, `profile`, `email`, `gmail.send`. The principle of minimal scope applies: a client should request only the scopes it actually needs, not "everything just in case," because each additional scope adds consent friction and blast radius if the token is stolen. The resource server must enforce scopes on every request — a token with `calendar.read` must be rejected for a write operation. Real-world examples: Google's "Sign in with Google" button requests `openid email profile` (three scopes for federated login, no API access); Gmail distinguishes `gmail.readonly` from `gmail.send` so a mail-merge tool can send without reading inbox contents. Scopes are surfaced as human-readable descriptions on the consent screen, which is why scope naming and per-app review matter for trust.
**Visual:**
```
client requests: scope="calendar.read profile"
   |
   v
consent screen: "App X wants to: see your calendars, see your profile"
   |
   v
access_token.scope = "calendar.read profile"
   |
   v
resource server: reject write (no calendar.write in scope)
```

### Q6. What is the difference between an access token and a refresh token in OAuth 2.0?
**Answer:** Access tokens are short-lived (typically 5–60 minutes) credentials presented to the resource server on every API call, usually as a `Bearer` token in the `Authorization` header. They are typically JWTs signed by the authorization server so the resource server can verify them offline, though opaque tokens validated via introspection (RFC 7662) are also valid. Refresh tokens are long-lived (days to weeks) credentials used to silently obtain new access tokens without re-prompting the user. Refresh tokens are server-side and revocable — when a user logs out, an admin disables the account, or token theft is detected — which is the only way to "log out" a user from an OAuth session short of waiting for the access token to expire. Refresh-token rotation, where each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, adds theft detection: replay of a stolen old refresh token triggers revocation of the entire session family. Access tokens are exposed on every API call and must be short-lived; refresh tokens are exchanged only at the token endpoint and can be long-lived if hardened.
**Visual:**
```
access token:  short (5-60 min), Bearer on every API call, often JWT
               exposed on wire, so MUST be short-lived
refresh token: long (days-weeks), only sent to /token endpoint
               server-side, revocable, rotated to detect theft
```

### Q7. What is the most common OAuth 2.0 implementation vulnerability, and how do you prevent it?
**Answer:** The most common vulnerability is redirect-URI manipulation. The authorization server redirects the user back to the client's `redirect_uri` with the authorization code in the URL; if the server matches redirect URIs permissively (e.g., prefix match, subdomain wildcard), an attacker can register a URI like `https://attacker.com.evil.com/callback` that matches the rule and intercept the code. Combined with a missing `state` parameter or a leaked client secret, the attacker can redeem the code and obtain tokens. The mitigations, codified in RFC 9700, are: exact-match redirect URIs (no wildcards); always use PKCE so a stolen code cannot be redeemed; always include and verify a `state` parameter as a CSRF token; never put access tokens in URLs (use the back channel for the token exchange); store tokens in HttpOnly cookies or platform keystores, never localStorage; never log tokens. Other common vulnerabilities include scope confusion (resource server does not validate scopes), token leakage in logs and referrers, and open-redirect chains.
**Visual:**
```
BAD:  redirect_uri match: prefix "https://app.example.com/"
      attacker registers "https://app.example.com.evil.com/cb"
      -> code intercepted
GOOD: redirect_uri: exact match only
      + PKCE (stolen code useless)
      + state (CSRF token verified)
      + back-channel token exchange (no token in URL)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are building a third-party app that integrates with Gmail to send mail on behalf of users. Which OAuth flow and scopes do you choose?
**Answer:** Use the authorization code flow with PKCE, because this is a user-facing client and PKCE is required by Google for SPA and mobile clients as of 2023. The user clicks "Connect Gmail"; you redirect them to Google's `/authorize` endpoint with `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope=gmail.send`, `state=<csrf>`, and `code_challenge=<pkce>`. The user logs in at Google and approves the `gmail.send` scope; Google redirects back to your `redirect_uri` with a code; you exchange the code plus your PKCE verifier (and your client secret, since this is a confidential server-side client) at Google's `/token` endpoint for an access token and refresh token. Crucially, request only `gmail.send`, not `gmail.readonly` or `https://mail.google.com/` (full access) — minimal scope reduces blast radius if the token leaks and reduces consent friction. Store the refresh token server-side, use it to silently obtain short-lived access tokens for each send, and provide a "Disconnect" button that revokes the token via Google's `/revoke` endpoint.
**Visual:**
```
user clicks "Connect Gmail"
   |
   v
/authorize?scope=gmail.send + PKCE   (NOT gmail.readonly)
   |
   v
exchange code -> access_token (1h) + refresh_token (7d, server-side)
   |
   v
each send: silent refresh if needed, then POST /gmail/v1/messages/send
   |
disconnect: POST /revoke?token=refresh_token
```

### Q2. A user reports that a malicious app obtained their Google Drive data without consent. How do you investigate?
**Answer:** First, ask the user to immediately revoke the malicious app's access at https://myaccount.google.com/permissions — this invalidates the refresh token, capping further access to the lifetime of any already-issued access token (typically 1 hour). Second, ask Google (via the user's account activity or your own audit logs if you are the resource server) which scopes the app was granted and when consent was given — most "unauthorized access" reports turn out to be consent screens the user clicked through without reading, not actual breaches. Third, if consent was genuinely not from the user, investigate whether the account was compromised and have them reset their password and enroll MFA. Fourth, if a redirect-URI or scope-confusion vulnerability on a legitimate OAuth integration was exploited, file a bug report with the provider and rotate any leaked tokens. Long term, deploy periodic permission-review reminders.
**Visual:**
```
report: "app got my Drive data without consent"
   |
   v
1. revoke app at myaccount.google.com/permissions
2. check granted scopes + consent timestamp
   |
   was consent real? YES -> user education (read the screen)
                  NO  -> account compromise? reset pw + MFA
                         OR integration bug? report + rotate
   |
annual permission review reminder to all users
```

### Q3. Your SPA was using the implicit flow and returning tokens in the URL fragment. How do you migrate to authorization code with PKCE?
**Answer:** The implicit flow was deprecated because tokens in URL fragments leak via browser history, referrer headers, and proxy logs, and because implicit cannot issue refresh tokens safely. Migrating requires three changes. First, change the `/authorize` URL: instead of `response_type=token`, use `response_type=code`, and add `code_challenge` and `code_challenge_method=S256`. Generate a random `code_verifier` per request, store it in memory (not localStorage), and compute the challenge as `base64url(sha256(verifier))`. Second, add a back-channel token exchange — because SPAs cannot hold a client secret, you exchange the code with just the PKCE verifier (the AS must allow public clients with PKCE). Third, add silent-refresh logic: when the access token expires, use the refresh token to obtain a new one without re-prompting. Store tokens in memory or, better, in HttpOnly cookies set by a backend-for-frontend (BFF) pattern. Google, Microsoft, and Auth0 all provide migration guides.
**Visual:**
```
old (implicit):  /authorize?response_type=token
                 -> access_token in URL fragment (leaks)
new (auth code + PKCE):
  /authorize?response_type=code&code_challenge=...
  -> code in URL (safe, single-use, PKCE-protected)
  -> back-channel /token exchange -> access + refresh
  -> silent refresh using refresh token
  -> tokens in memory or BFF (never localStorage)
```

### Q4. You are building a CLI tool that needs to authenticate users to your SaaS API. Browser-based OAuth is awkward for a CLI. What do you do?
**Answer:** Use the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant (RFC 8628), the same flow used by `gcloud`, `gh`, and `aws sso login`. The CLI displays a short user code (e.g., "ABCD-1234") and a verification URL, opens a browser for the user to authenticate at the IdP, and polls the token endpoint every 5 seconds until the user completes authentication or the code expires (typically 15 minutes). The CLI never sees the user's password, the access token is scoped and short-lived, and a refresh token is issued for subsequent silent refresh. For service accounts that cannot perform interactive login (e.g., a CI/CD pipeline), use the client credentials flow with a narrowly-scoped service account whose credentials are stored in a secrets manager. Either way, store tokens in the OS keychain rather than plaintext files.
**Visual:**
```
CLI                       AS
 |---device code request-->|
 |<--user_code + URL--------|
 | show user_code           |
 | poll /token every 5s    |
                          user opens browser, logs in, enters code
 |<--access + refresh token|
   |
store tokens in OS keychain
```

### Q5. Your mobile app uses OAuth with a custom URL scheme (`myapp://callback`) for the redirect. Security review flags it. What is the risk and the fix?
**Answer:** Custom URL schemes (`myapp://`) are vulnerable to interception on mobile platforms: any other app on the device can register the same scheme, and on Android (historically) and some iOS configurations, the OS may route the redirect to the attacker's app, allowing it to capture the authorization code. With PKCE the attacker still cannot redeem the code (lacking the verifier), but they could relay it. The modern fix is to use App Links (Android) and Universal Links (iOS), which bind a redirect URI to a specific app via a verified HTTPS domain — the OS checks the website's `/.well-known/assetlinks.json` (Android) or apple-app-site-association (iOS). Alternatively, use the PKCE-only flow with a loopback redirect (`http://127.0.0.1:port/callback`). Auth0, Google, and Microsoft all support App Links / Universal Links. Always use PKCE in addition.
**Visual:**
```
BAD:  redirect_uri = myapp://callback
      any app can register the scheme -> intercept code
GOOD: redirect_uri = https://app.example.com/callback
      + App Links (Android) / Universal Links (iOS)
      + assetlinks.json binds domain to app signature
      + PKCE (defense in depth)
```

### Q6. Your service calls another internal service using OAuth. Should you use the client credentials flow or pass through the user's access token?
**Answer:** It depends on whether the downstream service needs to enforce per-user authorization. If the downstream service only needs to know "a call from a trusted internal service" (e.g., a billing service querying a pricing service with no per-user concept), use the client credentials flow — the calling service obtains its own access token scoped to its own identity, with no user involved. This is simpler and decouples the services from user sessions. If the downstream service needs to enforce per-user authorization (e.g., an orders service calling a payments service on behalf of a specific user), you have two options: (1) forward the original user's access token (token relay), which works only if the downstream service trusts the same authorization server and scopes; or (2) exchange the user's token for a downstream-scoped token via token exchange (RFC 8693), which lets the authorization server issue a new token scoped specifically for the downstream service with the original user preserved as the actor. Token exchange is the cleaner pattern for service meshes and is used by SPIFFE, AWS STS, and GCP Workload Identity.
**Visual:**
```
no per-user authz needed:
  service A --client_credentials--> service B (knows "from A")

per-user authz needed:
  user token --relay--> service B (trusts same AS + scopes)
  OR
  user token --token_exchange (RFC 8693)--> downstream-scoped token
                                              (preserves user as actor)
```

### Q7. Your OAuth client stores access tokens in localStorage. Security review flags this. What do you change?
**Answer:** localStorage is accessible to any JavaScript running on the page, so a single XSS vulnerability exfiltrates every user's token. The fix depends on the client architecture. For server-rendered apps or any app with a backend, use the BFF (backend-for-frontend) pattern: the backend holds the tokens in a server-side session, and the browser holds only an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict session cookie. API calls go through the BFF, which attaches the access token server-side, so the token never reaches the browser. For pure SPAs with no backend, store tokens in memory only — they survive page refresh via silent refresh using a refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie. Either way, never use localStorage or sessionStorage for tokens. Additionally, set a short access-token lifetime (15 minutes), use refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, and add a strict CSP. Auth0, Microsoft, and Google all recommend the BFF pattern for production SPA deployments.
**Visual:**
```
BAD:  access_token in localStorage -> XSS exfiltrates it
GOOD: BFF pattern
        browser <--HttpOnly cookie--> BFF (server-side session)
        BFF      <--access token------> API
        token never reaches browser
ALSO: short access TTL (15 min)
      refresh-token rotation + reuse detection
      strict CSP to reduce XSS surface
```
